leftEvidence.title: Nathan’s story turns David’s judgment on himself

points.label: Action and response
points.left: Nathan tells of a rich man taking a poor man’s ewe, David condemns the act, Nathan says “You are the man,” recounts gifts and taking, announces consequences, and receives confession.
points.right: David fasts and lies on the ground while the child lives; after death he washes, worships, eats, answers his servants, comforts Bathsheba, and a son named Solomon is born and loved.

points.label: Evidence boundary
points.left: The source places David becomes the judged figure inside the story he judged inside this David setting without explaining every motive, transition, or later consequence.
points.right: The source places grief changes its bodily form after the child’s death while another son is born inside this David setting without explaining every motive, transition, or later consequence.

payload.posture: 2 Samuel 12:1–15 and 2 Samuel 12:16–25 are distinct approved David Scenes in the authored “Taking, Rebuke, and House Fracture” movement; holding them together exposes what continues and what changes without collapsing their sources.

rightEvidence.title: The child dies, David rises, and Solomon is born

payload.tension: 2 Samuel 12:1–15 foregrounds David becomes the judged figure inside the story he judged; 2 Samuel 12:16–25 foregrounds grief changes its bodily form after the child’s death while another son is born. Their sequence does not by itself explain every change between them.
payload.title: Nathan’s story turns David’s judgment on himself / The child dies, David rises, and Solomon is born
